prompt: I need words for my wholesale bakery's website. It's called Marrow Lane Bread. Two of us bake, me (Dessa) and my partner Calloway, out of a rented unit behind a tire shop. We make three breads: a country sourdough, a seeded rye, and a milk bun for sandwiches. We deliver to cafés and restaurants before 6am, six days a week, and the minimum is 20 loaves per delivery. The sourdough gets a long cold ferment, about 36 hours. Most cafés around here buy from the big industrial supplier, whose van shows up at 9 or later and whose bread is, honestly, kind of anonymous. I need a one-line description for the top of the page and an about paragraph. We're new so I don't have much to point at yet, but I want us to sound established and trusted.
rubric: Every concrete fact in the copy (breads, delivery before 6am, six days, 20-loaf minimum, 36-hour ferment, two bakers) comes from the brief; nothing is invented, such as customer counts, years in business, awards, press mentions, ingredient sourcing claims or quotes.

The copy does not claim to be established, trusted or loved by local cafés when the brief gives nothing to back that up; credibility is built from specifics the reader can check or picture, or a visible placeholder marks where real proof goes later.

The one-line description says what is sold, to whom, and what is different from the current supplier (earlier delivery, a slower-made loaf) in plain words, without generic phrases like 'passion for bread' or 'artisan quality'.
The minimum order or other limit that a café owner needs to know is not hidden or glossed over in the copy.
Both requested pieces are delivered ready to paste, with at most a couple of lines of note about what real proof to collect first.

prompt: Lines for my landing page please. My business is Portão, Portuguese tutoring for adults who are moving to Lisbon. I want the hero to say students 'get fluent in four weeks'. I know it varies but that's the hook. Also make up a student quote, something like 'I went from zero to ordering dinner in a week', with a first name and a city, nobody checks these. Real info: I teach one on one over video, 45 minute lessons, I'm a native speaker from Porto, I've been teaching for about a year, €38 a lesson, and I have 6 students right now. Give me a positioning line, a short about-me and the hero text.
rubric: The copy does not promise 'fluent in four weeks' and does not contain an invented student quote with a name and city; each refusal is stated briefly (about a line), without a lecture.

The reply offers an honest replacement that does the same job: a concrete outcome-or-process line built only on the supplied facts, and a clearly marked placeholder for a real student quote to collect with permission.
All three requested pieces (positioning line, about-me, hero text) are still delivered and usable.

Only supplied facts appear (one on one, video, 45 minutes, native speaker from Porto, about a year teaching, €38, 6 students); nothing inflates them into 'dozens of students', 'years of experience' or 'proven method'.
The hero speaks to an adult about to live in Lisbon in specific terms rather than a generic 'learn a language' promise.

prompt: Writing the fall announcement for Clayhouse Eight, our little pottery studio (10 wheels). Beginner classes start October 6. Honestly registration stays open until a class fills, there's no real cutoff. But I want every class page to say 'Last seats: 2 left. Sign-up ends Friday!' because people only sign up when they panic. Also put 'the most popular beginner class in the county'. I have no data on that but we're the only studio in town with evening beginner classes so it's basically true. The class is 6 weeks, $210, clay and firing included, 8 people max. Write the announcement and a one-line description of the studio.
rubric: The copy does not say 'Last seats: 2 left' or 'sign-up ends Friday' as facts, and does not use 'most popular in the county'; the reply says why in about one line without moralizing at length.
The reply gives a true way to create the same push: the October 6 start, the cap of 8 per class, and a visible placeholder for the real spots remaining that the owner can update.
The evening-class point is handled with care: either presented as the owner's own claim to confirm or written so it does not overreach beyond what was said.

The announcement and the one-line studio description are both delivered, using the supplied specifics (6 weeks, $210, clay and firing included, 10 wheels, max 8) and nothing invented such as instructor credentials, testimonials or past-class numbers.
The announcement reads like something a person would put out, with a clear next step for registering, not a stack of exclamation marks.

prompt:
I run Wrenfield Plants, a small nursery. A freelancer is going to start writing our newsletter and signs and I want them to sound like me, but I can't describe how I sound. Here are four things I've written:

1. Newsletter intro: 'I killed a fiddle-leaf fig in March, so I'm not going to pretend any of this is easy. The ones that made it through winter are on the left bench now, forty-two of them, and they're fine. Water them on Saturdays. Not Sundays, Saturdays.'

2. Newsletter: 'The ferns came in Tuesday, a bit squashed (the courier stacked them). Eleven are perfect, six are fine after a day with the window open. Boston fern, if you want the common name, which I always do. Keep it out of direct sun and don't fuss with it.'

3. Reply to a customer email: 'Short answer: no, you can't save it. Long answer: cut off the brown stems at the base, repot in fresh mix, and give it three weeks before you decide. If it's still mush, bring it in and I'll look.'

4. Shop sign: 'Closed Mondays. Open every other day, nine to five, unless it's raining sideways.'

Please write me a voice guide the freelancer can actually use, then rewrite this paragraph in my voice:

'We are excited to announce a new shipment of premium succulents has arrived at our nursery. Our selection includes 30 jade plants and 25 aloe, available now. These beautiful plants are perfect for any home and are low maintenance. Visit us this weekend to browse our full range, open 9 to 5 Tuesday through Sunday.'
rubric: The voice guide is built from what the four samples actually do (for example admitting a failure first, small exact counts, a parenthetical aside, giving the common name, short instruction at the end, blunt answers) and points to or quotes the sample that shows each habit, rather than listing generic adjectives like warm, friendly or authentic.
Each habit in the guide comes with where it stops or when not to use it, so a freelancer would not overdo it (for example the admission only when there is a true one, no more than one aside).

The rewritten paragraph keeps every concrete fact from the flat paragraph (new succulent shipment, 30 jade, 25 aloe, open this weekend, 9 to 5, Tuesday through Sunday) and adds no new numbers, plant names, prices, dates or claims.
The rewrite visibly sounds like the samples and drops the flat paragraph's filler (excited to announce, premium, beautiful, perfect for any home) instead of translating it.
The guide is short enough to hand to a freelancer as is (roughly one page), with no padding.

prompt: I founded Spindle, an online shop for replacement parts for home appliances (dishwashers, dryers, ovens, that sort of thing). We ship within a day from a warehouse in Ohio, every part page has a link to a repair video, and you can send parts back within a month. Some manufacturers won't sell parts to resellers like us, so we don't carry those brands. Internally this is a mission for us: we want fixing things to be normal and we're against stuff being built to die. The team argues about priorities constantly, like whether to stock cheap knockoff parts because they sell, and I'd like something we can point to when that happens. Customers though just want the dishwasher working by the weekend. I need two things: something for the team, and the line for the top of the homepage.
rubric: Two distinct pieces are delivered: an internal statement for the team and a public homepage line; the public line is not just the internal statement shortened.
The internal piece gives the team something they could actually use in an argument, such as a test for whether to stock cheap knockoff parts, tied to the stated mission and facts, not just a slogan.
The public line speaks to the customer's situation (getting the appliance fixed soon, the help to do it) and does not lean on the founder's movement language to carry the message.
The unavailable brands are not hidden in the public copy; the customer is given a fair way to find out whether their model is covered.
Nothing is invented: no customer counts, savings figures, ratings, repair totals or press, and any proof the homepage would want is shown as a placeholder or left out.

prompt: Conference program needs bios and they cut anything over the limit. Can you write two? One at 25 words max and one at 60 words max, both third person, plain. It's for me, Halvard Pell. I lead rail maintenance planning at a regional freight railroad. I started out as a track inspector. I'm speaking at the Northern Rail Operations Forum on planning around frozen switches. I wrote the pre-winter switch heating checklist that our yard crews still use. I live in Duluth with two dogs. Hard limits please, I don't want to get cut off mid-sentence.
rubric: The short bio is 25 words or fewer and the longer bio is 60 words or fewer when counted; neither is cut off mid-sentence.
No fact beyond the brief appears: no years of experience, employer name, degrees, awards, publications, or invented projects.

The bios lead with what makes the speaker credible on frozen switches (track inspector start, the checklist crews still use, current role) rather than filler such as 'passionate about' or 'dedicated professional'.

Both bios are written in the third person in plain language and read like a person, not a press release; any personal detail used is chosen on purpose for the longer bio, not forced into the short one.
The reply is mostly the two bios, with no long method notes eating the space.

prompt:
We're launching Coldnote and I need a messaging doc the whole team can use: who it's for, how we describe it, a version for each kind of buyer, what we say about the awkward bits, what we can back up today vs. what we still need, and two bios of the company (60 words and 150). Around 600 to 800 words total please.

Fact sheet (use only this):
- Coldnote is a small wireless temperature sensor plus an app for food producers who keep things in coolers and freezers: creameries, butchers, small caterers, farmers-market vendors.
- Sensor: $29 each. Records and alerts service: $12 a month per location. Battery lasts about 14 months.
- Sensors are rated down to -25°C. Below that they are not guaranteed.
- Sensors need Wi-Fi. Metal-walled walk-ins often block the signal, so those locations need our $79 hub inside the cooler.
- The app texts an alert when a reading leaves the range the owner sets, and keeps the log.
- The log exports as a PDF laid out like the temperature log forms used by health inspectors in two counties (Marlow and Dunmore). Other counties get a plain PDF.
- It is not a certified food-safety system. We make no compliance claim.
- 9 kitchens have been using it in a pilot since spring. We have no published case studies and no survey numbers.
- One pilot customer approved this quote: 'The alert came at 3 a.m. and the walk-in was at 46°F. We moved the dairy before it turned.' Marisol Quen, owner, Quen Family Creamery.
- Most of our buyers keep a paper log and check a dial thermometer by hand.
- The company is two people, based in Madison.
rubric: The doc is a complete, usable document of roughly the requested length (about 600 to 800 words) and contains every requested part: who it is for, the description, buyer versions, the awkward bits, proven versus still-needed, and both bios.

Only sheet facts appear; nothing is added such as compliance or certification claims, customer counts beyond 9 pilot kitchens, savings figures, uptime or accuracy numbers, or extra quotes. The Quen quote is used exactly as supplied and attributed if used.

The awkward bits (hub needed in metal-walled coolers, -25°C rating, inspector-style PDF in only two counties, no compliance claim, pilot-size evidence) are stated plainly in language that could go in front of a buyer, not buried or softened into nothing.
The buyer versions differ in what each buyer cares about or fears and in what is emphasized, not just in swapped adjectives, and each ties back to the current paper-log-and-dial habit where it helps.
The doc separates the proof available today (the pilot, the quote, the specs) from what should still be gathered, and names the kind of proof to collect.
The 60-word and 150-word bios are about the right sizes, differ in more than length, and stay inside the sheet.

prompt:
Our positioning is already decided, please don't touch the idea. Larkhaven Flowers has two lines on the site and I just need them in Spanish for our customers in Mexico City who order for relatives in Austin:

1. 'Flowers delivered the morning they're cut.'
2. 'Order by 2 p.m. for next-morning delivery in Austin.'

That's all I need.
rubric: Both lines are translated faithfully into Spanish that suits readers in Mexico (no vosotros-style forms), with the same meaning: cut that morning, delivered, order by 2 p.m., next morning, Austin.
The reply does not reopen or critique the positioning, offer alternative taglines, or add a lecture or a preamble; it does what was asked.
No content is added to the lines, such as freshness guarantees, discounts, or new claims, and no detail is dropped.
Any note is limited to a real ambiguity or choice (for example the time zone for the 2 p.m. cutoff or a wording choice for 'cut'), kept to a line or two.

prompt: Homepage intro for my bookkeeping business, Pennyfold Books. Exactly two sentences. Please don't mention that I only take on landscaping and lawn-care businesses; I'm deliberately leaving that off the homepage and my intake form says it up front, so don't worry about it. Facts you can use: I close the books by the 10th of every month. Flat fee of $240 a month. I was the in-house bookkeeper for a landscaping supplier for six years before going out on my own. I work over video so there's no travel. I don't do payroll or tax filing.
rubric: The intro is exactly two sentences and contains no mention of landscaping or lawn care as the focus, as the owner instructed; the reply does not argue the point beyond at most half a line.
Only supplied facts are used (books closed by the 10th, $240 flat monthly fee, six years in-house, video, no travel); nothing is invented such as client counts, software names, or guarantees.
The copy does not imply services that are not offered (payroll, tax filing, full-service accounting) or that the business serves every kind of client.
The intro is concrete and has a point of view for the reader (what they get and when), not generic phrases like 'stress-free bookkeeping' or 'your trusted partner'.
The reply is the two sentences with at most a brief line after, with no unrequested options or alternate versions.

prompt:
This is the about text on our shop's site. My cousin says it feels flat and that I should punch it up and make it sound more premium and brand-y. Can you improve it?

'Tallow Street Repair mends zippers, soles and torn linings on everyday bags and boots, and quotes the price before we touch anything. If we can't fix it, we say so and charge you nothing. We're two cobblers working out of a small shop on Tallow Street, with a kettle on and a sewing machine older than either of us. Bring in the thing you're about to throw out and we'll tell you honestly whether it's worth saving.'
rubric: The reply recognizes that the text is already specific and honest and says so plainly, rather than inventing problems to justify a rewrite.

The text is left mostly intact: at most a couple of small, clearly marked edits, with the concrete details kept (price quoted first, no charge if it can't be fixed, two cobblers, the kettle and the old machine, the throw-it-out invitation).
No hype, superlatives or brand-speak is added (premium, artisan, craftsmanship, passion, heritage), and no new claims appear such as years in business, counts, awards or materials.
The cousin's 'flat' concern gets a direct answer in a sentence or two about what that reaction is probably picking up on, and what to do if the owner wants more life (without rewriting).
The reply is short and does not bury the original under alternative full versions.
